S13v9-1P4: Along with that, you'll also need to budget for what the group can provide on the practical side. That is, the things they can offer in the way of water, housing, food stores, health care, tools, seasonal labor, transportation, schooling, market access, etc. If there are outside debts to pay or cash reserves, how long will the cash last? What are the few critical skills that could stop everything if nobody had them? It's boring stuff, I know. But in the end, a group could be great on an emotional level but be dead in the water because the well fails, or because one exhausted person is the only one who knows where everything is and how it works.
S13v9-4P2: There’s some correspondence first. Did they read the materials? (Not everyone does!) Do they get the basic idea of why this community is here? Are they at least starting to do the relevant practices? It’s a lot cheaper to find out through a thoughtful exchange than after six months of misunderstanding, right?
S13v9-4P1P2:
When The Farm grew fast, a lot of the people who came were in need, and there weren’t many filters that worked. Being open to everybody felt so spiritual! The practical burden piled up anyway. A membership process is there to protect both the people who are already there and the newcomers. It’s no good for anyone to join a group that can’t deliver what it promised.

S13v9-4P3P4:
The short visit: If they come for a week or two and just participate in normal life, well, most people can be charming for two weeks. So if that's all they do, congratulations! You've established that they can be charming for two weeks. 😅

The long visit: If you're not around long enough to actually experience inconvenience and conflict with the person in question, then you're not going to learn very much about them. Watch how they react when tired, corrected, attracted, disappointed, bored, etc. (Hopefully not all at once!) Even a professional faker may be able to pull off an act for months, so time gets you more evidence, not certainty.
S13v9-4P5: Have you thought about these questions: How long will a provisional membership be? What will a provisional member be responsible for and what are their rights? How will a provisional member's membership be reviewed? How might a person leave provisional membership? Who will make the decision about a person becoming a full member? (Hint: it shouldn't be the person who recruited them.) What rights will a full member have in terms of the land, other shared resources, and their voice within the group? What will a member be responsible for over the long term? (A full member's rights and responsibilities should be addressed in the agreements you draw up when you are first starting your group.) Yes, it's a lot of homework!
S13v9-4P9: Do visitors, volunteers, workers, renters and interns at a commune need some rights even if they're not fully "in" the commune politically? (Yes, even the interns!) When decisions really affect their pay or access to shared resources, they need clear terms and a way to be heard, and those decisions have to be open to review. Also when decisions really affect their schedule, safety, housing, records or discipline. Equality isn't just for members, or else there's a risk of recreating a servant class that moves from commune to commune.
